meta.title: Solo developer rebuilds Adobe Creative Suite in Rust using Claude, releases it free to all

comments.author: creesch
comments.text:
Let me fix that title


Solo developer rebuilds vibe codes buggy Adobe Creative Suite "alternative"  in Rust using Claude


I am not going to deny it is pretty impressive that current frontier models can create pretty good alpha level products. That doesn't mean it is actually an alternative as it is currently a buggy mess and with a lot of purely vibe coded products getting past that initial proof of concept and polishing it up to an actual solid working product is one of those things that remains illusive.

To get ahead of a certain crowd. No, I am not talking about you who actually looks at the output, reviews it and still applies fairly decent basic principles of software development. I am talking about vibe coding in the way it was originally coined, asking the model to do a thing and blindly trusting the output.

Which I have no issue claiming this product is when you see claims like " targets 100% parity in one month". There simply is no way to do this other than blindly trusting all your LLM tooling to work it out.

Edit:

Looking at the commit history shows how insane this is. Commits every few minutes simply means there is no human in the loop. It is all based on the hopes and dreams of people yelling into their prompts and telling the agents to please do a good job.

comments.author: teaearlgraycold
comments.text:
I find vibe coding to be sufficient for smaller projects where you can finish the entire project within a few hours or days. But I spend most of my time on QA. Human QA as well as LLM QA. Claude Opus 5.5 is actually pretty good at coming up with UI/UX/code QA issues. Almost all of the issues it finds are worth fixing - but it certainly is not finding all issues.

One task I've done a few times recently is ask Claude to open a web app in a headless browser and identify UI/UX issues. I have it then fix it and take cropped before/after screenshots. Finally I have it compose a self-contained webpage with every issue and the before/after images, problem statement, proposed solution, and code diff along with "Accept"/"Reject" buttons. 9/10 are both correctly identified issues and good solutions with clean code. I've done the same but with micro code refactors where I have it diagram the dependency tree changes.

For the couple of things I've recently vibe coded (although I do look at the code a bit, but less than I did a few months ago) it's like 40% of the time is adding features and 60% is QA.

comments.author: redwall_hp
comments.text:
Clean room reverse engineering is legal, yes. It's widely understood that having the same people do the reversal as the implementation from the derived spec is a good way to get your ass sued into the ground. (This goes way back to things like the cloning of the IBM PC: one team with a test bench poking signals into the system and taking readings, and a fully separate team using their written spec to build a compatible BIOS.)

A straight decompile and port into another language would still be infringing (just as publishing a translation of a novel is infringing). Decompilation is one thing that you never want to do while doing legal reverse engineering, because you're exposing yourself to implementational details.

If no decompilation happened, we get into the untested minefield of "is a leak of the source or a decompilation in the training set?" That's a risk. Any indication that code is sufficiently similar will be used as evidence of infringement.

Regardless, an individual probably can't afford to be sued by Adobe in the first place. This is exactly the kind of case I've been waiting for (though my money was on a Microsoft product)...if this were to go to court, it could establish case law that will make LLM use scarier to lawyers than GPL software. (And then they'll find out that they were trained on GPL code and often emit it verbatim...)

comments.author: creesch
comments.text:
It does not matter that the codebase is not maintainable by a person, as long as LLMs can maintain it, it will be fine.


That "as long as" is doing a hell of a lot heavy lifting here. What you are effectively advocating for is to have nobody understand the code base. LLMs don't have working memory or context awareness. All they have is the code and whatever is documented around that code. They too benefit from that code being structured and developed according to good practices. As it helps them write actual working functionality.

That structure is not there by default and by default most code hardnesses there is only a tiny amount of structure provided. Without anyone further dictating that structure you'll quickly end up with an amalgamation of different structures and approaches in your code base. This will be barely noticeable in small projects or early green field projects. But once a project grows it will become an issue as the LLM will start to confuse it self due to the code base containing all sorts of mixed signals it created itself.

Claiming you currently don't need to look at code is simply saying you don't care about overall quality. Or, somewhat more charitable, is based on you only inspecting small projects amd drawing conclusions from there.

comments.author: creesch
comments.text:
They can.


If you stretch the definition of "they can" then yes, they can. If you look at practical use, then for all intents and purposes they cannot.

Models perform worse with languages they have less training data for. Languages most common on GitHub like Python, JavaScript, Java, C++, etc generally show good performance where models score noticeably lower on things like Lua, R, Perl.

Frontier models tend to compensate for this by leaning on languages that look similar but that only goes as far. So no, if a language is not in the training data a model will not be able to work in it as fluently and, depending on the language struggle noticeably

Mind you, this is about languages they have been trained on. If they have no training data whatsoever for a language it will be even worse. Possibly you can compensate somewhat by having a prompt include "this language most closely relates to Y". But then you are also going to deal with a things like wrong assumptions about semantics, patterns that work slightly different causing issues, etc, etc.

Tool calls can help here but those are just a patch and will not yield the same results compared to a model natively having been trained on a language. It will also just mean more token consumption. And eat up a lot of your model's context window. Which matters more than you might realize as it is well documented that an advertised context window doesn't mean the model will perform as well with the entire window in use. Since there is no training data you'd need all relevant data always in that context window. Depending on the complexity this can mean a substantial use of the context window, resulting in additional degraded use. Improvements have been made here but this is also an area where open-weight models generally tend to trail behind, with a smaller effective context window than advertised.

So far I have just written about this in the context of one language even. Over times we are talking also about things like protocols, best practices, etc. Yes, you can put it all in tool calls, skills, etc. But again, that will not perform the same as the model having native base knowledge about a subject and at some point there will really be no effective context left to have it actually do the thing you want. You might say that it only needs to pull information in where it needs it, but if most of the project is something it has no data on that just means it has keep pulling in that data.

To sum it up, in the short term I'll hand it to you. Sure, small changes to frameworks and languages initially you'd be able to compensate for with some small degradation in performance. In the long term, no they effectively cannot.

As far as fine tuning goes, it effectively has a similar problem. Tuning is good at changing behavior and style, less so at adding new information to a model that was not included in pre-training. Knowledge added through fine tuning is something models tend to hallucinate more over, to the point that retrieval (so the earlier mentioned tool calls) is seen as more effective. Which, in itself already has limitations as I went over.

Fine tuning also tends to change models overall degrading some things they already "know" which only gets worse every time you tune a model again. Talking about years of drift and multiple fine tuning rounds and I guess you'll have the next generation meme about model rot the same way people meme about JPEG artifacts.

Then there is the practical aspect of it all. It is one thing to tune a model on one additional subject. That's not going to be the case though, it will not just be one language or one framework but all additional data and knowledge I already mentioned earlier. Even if fine tuning was without flaws it would be a massive undertaking to keep models up to date on all of that (or even a subset). As it stands fine tuning is not up to task of doing the same sort of training that these labs do. And no, the popular narrative that the Chinese labs are doing this with barely any budget isn't quite true.

Which returns me to my original point. Open weight models are also heavily subsidized at the moment, without millions invested in hardware to train these models it currently isn't possible to reproduce their results. And as I hopefully have made clear now, the current models will not remain usable no matter what, yes you can keep running them, I am talking practical usage. That also means, that from my perspective, the entire LLM industry can effectively rug pull us as consumers. Not just the frontier labs by raising pricing, but also the Chinese labs by simply no longer providing these models for free. We could hope they'd offer them for less than the frontier labs, but that is also not a given.

I honestly think it is better to be realistic about this. And to be extra clear, I am not coming at this from a perspective of someone against the use of LLMs in general. I happily use them in all sorts of tasks. I am also acutely aware that the current situation isn't likely to last and that it might mean a significantly higher cost of using them in the future. I rather be wrong about that than to be wrong about firmly believing everything will be well in the future and nothing is really going to change.

1.1 Avoiding GIMP's hole
The criticism of GIMP is historically true, and much of it still applies in 2026.

Bit depth.

GIMP's original core hard-coded 8-bit-per-channel tiles.
High bit depth needed a whole new engine, GEGL. GEGL began around 2000, was introduced as optional in 2.6 (2008), and the port only finished in GIMP 2.10 (2018), "the result of six years of work" on that port alone.
Only then did GIMP get 16/32-bit integer and float processing.
Non-destructive editing.

Photoshop has had adjustment layers since about 1994.
GIMP got non-destructive filters in 3.0 (March 2025), about seven years after 2.10 because of the GTK3 port.
It got non-destructive layer types (link layers, vector layers) in 3.2 (March 2026).
CMYK.

GIMP 3.x is still "a 100% RGB editor" internally.
CMYK exists only as export (JPEG/TIFF/PSD) and soft-proofing.
PSD.

Import is still lossy. Photoshop adjustment layers and most layer styles are not carried over faithfully, and text often needs re-typing.
3.2 converts legacy drop and inner shadows into GIMP filters, and added PSB export.


That isn't really isn't something you'd instruct the agent to if it were actually just does a transpilation. It's not like you can accidentally become GIMP doing that. You'd only need this when you're doing it from scratch and really, really don't want it to accidentally become GIMP.

comments.author: balooga
comments.text:
I mean, does that make it not true?

The industry is changing. These things don’t happen all at once or in every company according to a common timeline. Some people will feel the effects before others do, and that’s largely a matter of luck.

My SE career of 18 years ended last year when I and many in my department were unceremoniously laid off. I thought my department head was being unusually gruff when he gave me the bad news and bolted, only later did I learn that he’d been given the axe himself moments before, and his final duty with the company was to do the same to his subordinates. A shitty day all around. AI was never the stated reason, just nebulous “restructuring.” Okay. We were early adopters of Claude Code, so it was at least a factor, but saying more than that is idle speculation.

Anyway, I had already been grappling with career burnout for a few years. The work just wasn’t fun like it had been a decade before. It paid well, but (particularly after the pandemic killed off IRL coworker friendships and cool office perks) it was losing its luster. Then the introduction of Claude workflows redefined my role from a solution finder to a prompt-writer and AI babysitter. I was growing steadily less satisfied with that lot by the time the layoff came, and that was the final straw for me. Of course, I still had to look for new work.

When I re-entered the tech job market I noticed a lot of things were different from the last time I had been there:


Most of the roles now had “Agentic” or “AI-native” in the title. These were prompt-writing and AI babysitting jobs. Not what I ever signed up for or was good at.

Constant ghosting is apparently the norm now. Supposedly that’s because companies are overrun with LLM-slop applications and can’t sort the signal from the noise; also I guess a lot of job boards are now filled with fake ads and scams so the problem is multiplied. Very seldom did I hear back from any listing I applied to.

Pay on offer was notably reduced, across the board, from what I’d been making for years.

One of the things I’ve come to dread the most in job hunting life is the tech interview loop. I’ve been through too many to count, over the years, and have some real trauma from them. I’m not sure how the AI era has changed them, because I didn’t make it that far with anyone this time around. Felt like a slap in the face after all the years of hard work I’ve done.


Anyway to make a long story short, I pivoted. Left the tech sector entirely, and I’m happier for it. I got an administrative job at a large public university. Now I’m doing work that directly helps students. I meet with them and solve problems for them and I get to see the gratitude on their faces. I never got that from any of my old jobs, where I was kept as far away from humans as possible and the ultimate goal of every task I completed was just to make arrow go up.

I’m making about 1/4 of what I used to make, which legitimately sucks, but I’m happy with what I’m doing. Compared to constantly reviewing Claude’s verbose PRs, which were always so confident yet wrong in subtle but critical ways… this new job is mentally so much easier. And my non-technical coworkers think I’m a genius when I show them how to update their email signatures, lol. I feel appreciated, and for once like I might have lasting job security too.

A nice bonus is that I do have access to basically unlimited AI resources, courtesy of the university. So I’m able to keep up with the tech (which is still interesting to me) at no personal cost, and research uses for it on my own terms, to build things that help people, with no PMs breathing down my neck or KPIs driving everything I do. I’m pleased with how things worked out.

But, to summarize — I absolutely do credit AI’s impact on the tech industry as the killing blow to my SE career. I think maybe it hit me earlier than others (including those it’s still coming for but hasn’t reached yet), just because of the nature of my preexisting burnout and middle age long career history. I think many in the field will remain employed, but have to accept that the work they’re doing is irreversibly changing. Maybe they’ll like it better this way, I didn’t. I don’t know what the future holds for me or my SE compatriots, but I can say right now that I’m glad I got out.

There are shifts and then there are trends. Tech has had plenty of trends that for a while disrupted the ability for other sub-sectors to do their duty (see: big data the decade before, and mobile some 15-20 years ago. Oh, and a little thing called the dotcom age).

Trends can indeed become a shift, but never at the same time. The dotcom bubble was a trend ultimately stabilizing, but it didn't kill off the idea of a website fronted. It created new workflows and new dedicated roles.  NFT's, meanwhile, was very much a trend that fizzed out to little affair.

Us still talking about how "everything is changing" but not about the actual tangible changes very much proves we're in "trend" mode. How will that evolve if/when the bubble bursts? No clue, it's anyone's guess. Not much can change, we may instead ditch giant frontier models for lean open weight models. Nothing is set in stone, though. That's for sure. Last year people were gloating about how they never needed to code again, and then token-based pricing quickly had those reigns pulled in.
